pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 7-8. Understand that the multiples of 100 (100, 200 … 900) are 'some hundreds with 0 tens and 0 ones' — 300 = 3 hundreds, 0 tens, 0 ones. This isolates the hundreds column and reinforces two placeholder zeros.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 3): 'count from 0 in multiples of 4, 8, 50 and 100'; three-digit place value (hundreds, tens, ones).
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.NBT.1b 'the numbers 100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600, 700, 800, 900 refer to one, two, three… nine hundreds (and 0 tens and 0 ones)'.
• Operational details — Build multiples of 100 from hundred-flats only, pairing with skip-counting in 100s and placement on a 0-1000 number line. Emphasise the DOUBLE placeholder (two zeros) and connect to the analogous decade structure (300 is to hundreds what 30 is to tens). Read and write them and locate them as landmark numbers.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 7, emerging): builds 500 with 5 flats, says 'five hundreds'. Tier B (age 7-8, secure): reads/writes any multiple of 100 and explains the two zeros. Tier C (age 8, extending): places multiples of 100 on a 0-1000 line and links them to the tens/decade pattern.
bestPractices: Build multiples of 100 from hundred-flats alone so 'pure hundreds, no tens, no ones' is visible — both empty columns justify the two zeros.
Skip-count in 100s aloud (100, 200, 300…) while placing flats, binding count to structure.
Explicitly parallel the decade pattern: 300 is 'three hundreds' as 30 is 'three tens' — the ×10 self-similarity again.
Use the 0-1000 number line to treat multiples of 100 as landmark/benchmark numbers for later estimation and rounding.
Contrast 300 with 30 and 3, and with 303/330, to sharpen the meaning of each zero.
keyRepresentations: Base-ten hundred-flats (multiples of 100 as pure hundreds)
H|T|O place-value chart with empty tens and ones columns
commonMisconceptions: Treating the two zeros as meaningless or writing 300 as 3 / 30.
Reading 300 as 'three-oh-oh' or as three separate digits.
Confusing multiples of 100 with multiples of 10 (300 vs 30).
Not connecting 'three hundreds' to the parallel 'three tens' pattern.
Placing multiples of 100 wrongly on the number line by ignoring magnitude.

learn.summary: For ages 7-8: understand that multiples of 100 (100, 200 … 900) each name a count of hundreds with 0 tens and 0 ones, so 300 = 3 hundreds, 0 tens, 0 ones. The focus is isolating the hundreds column, giving meaning to the two placeholder zeros, reading/writing these numbers as whole quantities, and placing them as landmarks on a 0-1000 line. Learners also connect the pattern to the familiar tens pattern (300 is to hundreds as 30 is to tens).

activities.title: Hundreds-only builder with live numeral and placeholder zeros
feedback: If a learner writes 300 as 3 or 30, rebuild it from 3 hundred-flats with nothing in tens or ones and point out that the empty columns ARE the zeros; contrast 3, 30, and 300 side by side on the chart.
If a learner reads the leading 3 as 'three' rather than 'three hundreds', name its place: '3 in the hundreds place means 3 hundreds, which is 300', and count the hundreds together.

If a learner reads 300 as 'three-oh-oh' or as three separate digits, read it as the single quantity 'three hundred', tying the 3 to the hundreds place and the two zeros to the empty tens and ones places.
When the tens-rod turns 300 into 310, highlight that the middle zero was holding that place open until something filled it.
activities.rationale: Building pure hundreds makes both empty columns concrete, so the double placeholder is felt rather than memorised; toggling a single tens-rod in and out demonstrates that the zero marks a genuine, currently-empty place. An optional synced numeral, a spoken skip-count, a Gattegno chart hundreds row, a bead string, and a number-line hop are examples of ways to bind the count to the structure, not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils 'count from 0 in multiples of 4, 8, 50 and 100' and work with three-digit place value.
The numbers 100, 200…900 refer to one to nine hundreds (and 0 tens and 0 ones) — 2.NBT.1b.
learnerActions: Build 100, 200, 300 … 900 using only hundred-flats placed in the hundreds (H) column of a place-value chart, leaving the tens (T) and ones (O) columns visibly empty.
Watch or write the numeral as each flat is added (100 → 200 → 300) and note that two zeros appear because the T and O columns hold nothing.
Add a single tens-rod to the empty tens column of 300 and observe the numeral change to 310, then remove it to return to 300.
Say aloud what each digit means, e.g. '300 is 3 hundreds, 0 tens, 0 ones', and read the whole number as 'three hundred'.

Skip-count in 100s aloud while building: 100, 200, 300 …; optionally track the same count on a Gattegno chart hundreds row (100, 200 … 900 = 'n hundreds') or a skip-counting bead string as alternative representations.
activities.intendedInsight: The two zeros in a multiple of 100 are not padding: they record that the tens and ones places are empty. When something is actually placed in the tens column, the zero is replaced, which shows the zero was holding a real place.

activities.title: Landmark family wall and number-line placement
feedback: If a multiple is placed out of order or in the wrong region, count the hundreds along the line together (100, 200, 300 …) to check magnitude.
If a learner confuses 300 with 30, locate both on the same 0-1000 number line and compare how far along each sits: 30 is very close to 0, while 300 is three hundred-marks along.
A static reference wall is useful for recognition and recall, but confirm understanding of the zeros through building or explanation, not just tapping.
activities.rationale: Treating multiples of 100 as benchmarks on a 0-1000 line links symbol to magnitude and builds the landmark intuition used in estimation and rounding. A reference chart supports recall but, on its own, does not require the learner to construct or justify the place-value structure.
sourceClaims: Multiples of 100 serve as landmark numbers on the number line supporting estimation and rounding.
learnerActions: Study a family chart of the multiples of 100 (each shown as its flats, its numeral, and the words 'n hundreds, 0 tens, 0 ones').
Tap or point to a chosen multiple (e.g. 400) and state how many flats it has and how many tens and ones (four hundreds, 0 tens, 0 ones).
Place 300, 500, 700, and 800 on a 0-1000 number line, using the hundred marks as labelled landmarks.
Order a scrambled set of multiples of 100 from smallest to largest.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiples of 100 are evenly spaced landmark numbers on the line to 1000; their position reflects their magnitude, which later supports estimation and rounding.

activities.title: Explain and consolidate the place-value structure
feedback: If a learner says the zeros are meaningless, revisit the builder: the empty tens and ones columns are exactly what the zeros record.
If a learner says '3 hundreds' but cannot say what the zeros contribute, ask them to add a ten or a one and watch which zero changes.
For 'how many tens in 300', support reasoning that 300 is 30 tens (each hundred is 10 tens) as an extension, distinct from the fact that the tens DIGIT is 0.
activities.rationale: Explanation and matching tasks consolidate and let a teacher check whether the zeros are understood as placeholders rather than ignored. Recognition and fill-in tasks assess and reinforce after teaching but do not by themselves elicit the independent construction that the builder provides.
sourceClaims: The numbers 100, 200…900 refer to one to nine hundreds (and 0 tens and 0 ones) — 2.NBT.1b.
learnerActions: Complete statements such as '300 = 3 hundreds, __ tens, __ ones'.
Match each multiple to its flats and to its words (e.g. 500 ↔ 5 flats ↔ 'five hundreds').
Answer: 'Why isn't 300 the same as 30?' and 'How many tens are there in 300?' with a reason.
Write 300 and explain in words what the 3 tells us and what the two 0s tell us.
Contrast 300 with 30, 3, 303, and 330 to say what each zero is doing.
activities.intendedInsight: Each digit's value depends on its place; the zeros in a multiple of 100 state that the tens and ones places are empty, which is what distinguishes 300 from 30 or 3.

constraints: Learners should build or construct multiples of 100 and explain the zeros, not only recognise or tap labels; recognition-only tasks do not elicit independent construction of the place-value structure.
A static family chart or reference wall supports recall and landmark recognition but cannot show the zeros toggling; pair it with building or explanation.
Distinguish the two senses of 'tens' in 300: the tens DIGIT is 0 (nothing in the tens place), while the number 300 equals 30 tens overall. Do not conflate these when answering 'how many tens in 300'.
Be precise that 300 ≠ 30 and 300 ≠ 3: the difference is which places are filled, shown by magnitude on the number line.
Number-line placement should reflect magnitude; check spacing/order rather than treating placement as decorative.
Read a multiple of 100 as a whole quantity ('three hundred'), never digit-by-digit as 'three-oh-oh'.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source lists the cited CCSS 2.NBT.1b claim and the NCETM landmark claim as verified:false; treat their support as unconfirmed and do not infer empirical efficacy from citation.

Self-audit: the original two-tier probe asks 'How many tens are there in 300?' while the main teaching correctly states the tens DIGIT is 0. These are different questions (tens place-value digit vs total count of tens = 30). The activity keeps both but flags the distinction to avoid teaching that '300 has 0 tens' in the counting sense.

The original rated conversation and 3D formats as 'poor' ('planar; no spatial payoff', 'open dialogue is a poor fit'). These are catalogue fit judgements, not pedagogical laws; discussion can still support explanation of the zeros, and such rankings were not propagated as universal claims.

The Gattegno chart hundreds row and bead string from the source representation inventory are reinstated as optional alternative skip-count representations, offered alongside (not in place of) the builder and number line.

probeDeeper: Place 300, 500 and 800 on a 0–1000 number line.
How many tens are there in 300?
assess.correctAnswer: The 3 means 3 hundreds (300); the two 0s show 0 tens and 0 ones, holding those places empty.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the zeros as meaningless and collapses the number: '300 is the same as 3'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build 300 with 3 hundred-flats, no tens, no ones; the empty tens and ones ARE the zeros. Contrast 3, 30, 300 on a place-value chart.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child ignores the zeros or equates 300 with 3.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the leading digit at face value: 'the 3 means three'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Give the digit its place ('3 in the hundreds place = 3 hundreds = 300') and count the hundreds on a 0–1000 line.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says the 3 stands for three rather than three hundreds.

responseLevels.gap: Reads the leading digit at face value or drops the placeholder zeros.
responseLevels.full: States 3 hundreds, 0 tens, 0 ones, explains the zeros hold the empty places, and locates multiples of 100 on a line.
responseLevels.partial: Says '3 hundreds' but is unsure what the zeros contribute.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Write 300. Ask: 'What is the 3 telling us, and what are the two 0s telling us? How do you know?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with hundreds place value reads '3 hundreds, 0 tens, 0 ones'; a face-value thinker says the 3 means three, and a zero-blind child collapses 300 to 3. The reason tier reveals whether the zeros are understood as placeholders.
